title: Why Foxes Pounce North-East: 73% vs 18%
description:
When a red fox dives into deep snow or tall grass for a mouse it can only hear, which way it faces seems to matter. Scientists in the Czech Republic watched 84 wild foxes make 592 mousing jumps. In high cover, jumps aimed roughly north-east (about 20° clockwise of magnetic north) caught prey about 73% of the time; jumps the opposite way did fairly well too, but most other directions managed just 18%. Wind, sun and time of day didn't explain it, and in short grass, where foxes could see their prey, direction didn't matter. The leading idea: Earth's magnetic field dips into the ground at about 60-70°, and a fox may use it as a rangefinder, creeping forward until the mouse's sound comes from that same angle. It's still a hypothesis: nobody has found a magnetic sense in foxes yet.
